subject: English
name: English, Year 7
syllabus: Victorian Curriculum F-10 Version 2.0: English, Level 7

points.title: Language and identity
points.brief: The words, slang, accent and level of formality people use show who they are and which groups they belong to.

points.title: Evaluative language
points.brief: Words that judge, such as brilliant, careless or unfair, show a writer's opinion, and some judge more strongly than others.

points.title: Backing up an opinion
points.brief: An opinion is more convincing when it is supported with reasons, examples and evidence, rather than stated on its own.

points.title: How purpose shapes structure
points.brief: A narrative, an information report, a persuasive text and a procedure are each organised differently because they do different jobs.

points.title: Language features change with purpose
points.brief: A report uses technical words and facts, a persuasive text uses emotive words and opinions, and a story uses description and dialogue.

points.title: Overviews, topic sentences and conclusions
points.brief: An overview tells the reader what is coming, a topic sentence states what a paragraph is about, and a conclusion draws the ideas together.

points.title: Compound and complex sentences
points.brief: A compound sentence joins two main clauses with a word such as and or but. A complex sentence adds a dependent clause beginning with a word such as because or although.

points.title: Compound-complex sentences
points.brief: A sentence with two or more main clauses and at least one dependent clause, used to link and explain several ideas at once.

points.title: Keeping tense consistent
points.brief: Staying in the past or the present tense throughout a piece, and only changing tense when the time really changes, keeps writing clear.

points.title: Colons and brackets
points.brief: A colon introduces a list, an example or an explanation. Brackets add extra information the sentence would still make sense without.

points.title: Everyday and technical meanings
points.brief: Some words mean one thing in everyday talk and another in a subject, such as cell, volume or table, and context shows which is meant.

points.title: Camera shots and angles
points.brief: Close-ups show emotion, long shots show setting, a low angle makes someone look powerful and a high angle makes them look small.

points.title: Sound in film
points.brief: Music, sound effects and silence shape how a scene feels, such as tense music building suspense before anything happens.

points.title: The context of a text
points.brief: When and where a text was written, and the culture and society around its author, shape its ideas, characters and events.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander literature
points.brief: Stories, poems and memoirs by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors often draw on connection to Country, family, language and long traditions of storytelling.

points.title: Narrative point of view
points.brief: A first-person narrator tells the story as I, a third-person narrator as he, she or they, and the choice changes what the reader knows.

points.title: Forming an opinion about a text
points.brief: A good opinion about a character or event names a clear view, gives reasons from the text, and allows that others may read it differently.

points.title: Showing character
points.brief: Writers reveal character directly by describing it, or indirectly through actions, dialogue, thoughts and how others react.

points.title: Setting and mood
points.brief: Where and when a story happens creates a mood, such as a storm adding fear, and can reflect what characters feel.

points.title: Plot structure
points.brief: Most stories move through an orientation, a complication, rising action, a climax and a resolution.

points.title: Types of conflict
points.brief: Conflict drives a story, whether a character struggles against another person, against nature, against society or within themselves.

points.title: Simile, metaphor and personification
points.brief: A simile compares using like or as, a metaphor says one thing is another, and personification gives human qualities to something that is not human.

points.title: Sound devices in poetry
points.brief: Alliteration repeats first sounds, assonance repeats vowel sounds, and onomatopoeia uses words that sound like what they name.

points.title: Rhyme and rhythm
points.brief: Rhyme links line endings, and rhythm is the beat made by stressed and unstressed syllables, which together give a poem its sound.

points.title: Lines, stanzas and free verse
points.brief: Poems are arranged in lines and stanzas, and free verse drops a regular rhyme and rhythm so line breaks do more of the work.

points.title: Features of voice
points.brief: Pace, volume, pitch, pauses and emphasis change how a spoken message comes across to listeners.

points.title: Formal spoken presentations
points.brief: A formal presentation uses a clear opening, organised points and a conclusion, with formal words suited to the audience.

points.title: How technology changes reading
points.brief: Online texts mix words, images, video and links, are often read by scrolling and skimming, and can be shared and answered at once.

points.title: Prefixes and suffixes
points.brief: A prefix such as un- or re- changes a word's meaning, and a suffix such as -ful or -ness can change what kind of word it is.

points.title: Greek and Latin roots
points.brief: Many English words are built on Greek and Latin roots, such as graph (write) and port (carry), which help with meaning and spelling.

points.title: Spelling rules for adding endings
points.brief: Common patterns such as doubling the last consonant (run, running), dropping a silent e (make, making) and changing y to i (happy, happiness).

points.title: Audience and purpose
points.brief: Writers choose words, tone and detail to suit who will read the text and what it is meant to do, such as inform, persuade or entertain.

points.title: Ways of organising ideas
points.brief: Texts can be organised in time order, as causes and effects, or by sorting things into groups and types.

points.title: Making inferences
points.brief: An inference is a conclusion drawn from clues in the text and what the reader already knows, about something the text does not say outright.

points.title: Summarising
points.brief: A summary gives only the main ideas of a text in your own words, much shorter than the original and without small details.

points.title: Choosing a text type
points.brief: Matching the form of a text, such as a letter, report, speech or story, to its purpose and audience.

points.title: Multimodal texts
points.brief: A multimodal text combines two or more modes, such as words, images, sound and movement, which work together to make meaning.

points.title: Editing for impact
points.brief: Editing removes repetition, reorders sentences for flow and swaps weak words for precise ones, so the writing has more effect.
